summary: In 2018-2019, Canada-US trade relations were dominated by tariff disputes and renegotiation of NAFTA. In March 2018 the Trump administration imposed 25% tariffs on steel and 10% on aluminum from Canada, prompting Ottawa to retaliate with tariffs on US goods. On November 30, 2018, Canada, the US and Mexico signed the new USMCA (CUSMA) agreement, though the metal tariffs remained in place. On May 17, 2019, Canada and the United States reached a deal ending the steel and aluminum tariffs and Canada's retaliatory measures. The USMCA still required ratification by all three legislatures before taking effect.

Gender equality and pay equity were prominent topics in Canada in 2018-2019, amid the broader #MeToo movement. In 2018, the federal government introduced proactive pay equity legislation (part of Bill C-86), requiring federally regulated employers with 10 or more employees to close gender-based pay gaps; it received royal assent in December 2018, though regulations to implement it were still being developed into 2019. Equal Pay Day in 2019 marked the symbolic point in the year when women's average earnings caught up to men's earnings from the previous year. Debates over women's representation in politics and workplaces, and over the extent of ongoing gender discrimination, continued through the period.

Debates over free speech, protest and hate speech were active in Canada before May 2019. Federal Bill C-16, which added gender identity protections to human rights and hate-crime law, took effect in 2017 and remained a flashpoint, with figures like psychologist Jordan Peterson arguing it threatened free speech; his campus appearances were repeatedly disrupted by protesters. In Quebec, the government of Premier Francois Legault introduced Bill 21 on secularism on March 28, 2019, which would restrict public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols; the bill drew large protests in Montreal, including a march of thousands in April 2019, with critics calling it discriminatory and supporters calling it a defence of state neutrality.

Electoral reform remained a live issue in Canada after the Liberal government abandoned its 2015 promise to replace first-past-the-post voting. In February 2018, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said he would not revisit electoral reform unless other parties agreed on an alternative, which NDP and Green MPs criticized as a broken promise. A British Columbia referendum on proportional representation failed in December 2018, with about 60% of voters rejecting the change. With a federal election set for October 2019, parties' positions on voting-system reform, campaign finance, and foreign interference in elections continued to be discussed.

Federal politics in early 2019 was dominated by the SNC-Lavalin affair. In February 2019, the Globe and Mail reported that the Prime Minister's Office had pressured then-justice minister Jody Wilson-Raybould to help the Montreal engineering firm SNC-Lavalin avoid criminal prosecution over corruption charges tied to its dealings in Libya, in favour of a remediation agreement. Wilson- Raybould had been shuffled out of the justice portfolio in January 2019 and resigned from cabinet in February; fellow minister Jane Philpott also resigned in March 2019 in solidarity. Both were later expelled from the Liberal caucus. The affair dominated Parliament through spring 2019 ahead of the October federal election between Justin Trudeau's Liberals and Andrew Scheer's Conservatives.

Canada's relations with China deteriorated sharply after Canadian authorities arrested Huawei chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou in Vancouver on December 1, 2018, at the request of the United States, which sought her extradition on fraud charges linked to alleged sanctions violations. China denounced the arrest and, in apparent retaliation, detained two Canadians, Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor, on December 10, 2018, and in March 2019 accused them of stealing state secrets. China also blocked canola shipments from major Canadian exporters in March 2019. By May 2019, China's ambassador described bilateral relations as being at their "rock bottom" point since diplomatic ties began.

Immigration policy, especially irregular border crossings into Quebec, was a prominent issue before the 2019 election. Since 2017, tens of thousands of asylum seekers had crossed into Canada irregularly at Roxham Road, a de facto crossing point on the Quebec-New York border; in 2018 these interceptions numbered in the tens of thousands, producing a large backlog at the Immigration and Refugee Board, with wait times approaching two years. The federal government pledged $173 million to improve border security and speed claims processing, and offered compensation to nearby residents affected by the increased crossings. The issue was expected to feature prominently in Quebec during the fall 2019 campaign.

Quebec identity and secularism politics were prominent in spring 2019. Premier Francois Legault's Coalition Avenir Quebec government, elected in October 2018, introduced Bill 21 on March 28, 2019, which would ban public employees in positions of authority (such as teachers, police officers and judges) from wearing religious symbols while on duty. The bill prompted large protests in Montreal in April 2019 and strong criticism from federal party leaders and municipal officials, while the CAQ government defended it as upholding state secularism. Debate over Quebec's place in the federation and over bilingualism continued alongside the secularism debate.

Canada-US trade relations improved after a tense 2018. Following tit-for-tat tariffs on steel and aluminum imposed in 2018, Canada, the US and Mexico signed the new USMCA (CUSMA) trade agreement on November 30, 2018, replacing NAFTA. On May 17, 2019, Canada and the US reached an agreement ending the steel and aluminum tariffs and Canada's retaliatory tariffs. Through summer 2019, the USMCA still awaited ratification by the US Congress and other legislatures before entering into force, and the agreement was a backdrop to the fall 2019 Canadian federal election campaign that began on September 11, 2019.

Gender equality remained a salient issue heading into the fall 2019 federal election. Federal pay equity legislation, part of Bill C-86, received royal assent in December 2018 but was still being implemented through regulations in 2019. The #MeToo movement continued to shape discussion of workplace harassment and women's representation. Women held 26% of House of Commons seats following the 2015 election. On August 22, 2019, Public Safety Minister Ralph Goodale tweeted footage of a 2005 speech by Conservative leader Andrew Scheer opposing same-sex marriage, reviving the controversy as the fall 2019 campaign, which began September 11, approached; Scheer said he would not reopen the issue.
note: Corrected Scheer video controversy date (August 22, 2019, not September) and women's House of Commons seat share (26%, not ~27%).

summary: Free speech and protest debates continued through mid-2019. Quebec's Bill 21, banning religious symbols for public employees in positions of authority, was passed into law on June 16, 2019, by a 73-35 vote after the Coalition Avenir Quebec government invoked closure to speed debate; it had prompted large protests in Montreal earlier in the year and was challenged in court shortly after passage. Nationally, debates over hate-speech law (including Bill C-16's gender-identity protections) and campus free-speech controversies, such as disruptions of appearances by psychologist Jordan Peterson, continued to be discussed as the fall 2019 election campaign got underway.

Canada's 40-day federal election campaign began on September 11, 2019, with voting day set for October 21, 2019, between Justin Trudeau's Liberals and Andrew Scheer's Conservatives, along with the NDP, Greens and Bloc Quebecois. Electoral reform remained unresolved after the Liberals abandoned their 2015 promise to end first-past-the-post voting, a decision Trudeau defended in 2018 by saying no consensus existed on an alternative; a 2018 BC referendum on proportional representation had also failed. The SNC-Lavalin affair, which saw ministers Jody Wilson-Raybould and Jane Philpott resign from cabinet earlier in 2019, continued to weigh on perceptions of the governing Liberals as the campaign opened.

The 2019 federal election campaign formally began September 11, 2019, pitting Justin Trudeau's Liberals against Andrew Scheer's Conservatives, Jagmeet Singh's NDP, Elizabeth May's Greens and Yves-Francois Blanchet's Bloc Quebecois. The campaign followed the SNC-Lavalin affair, in which the Prime Minister's Office was alleged to have pressured former justice minister Jody Wilson-Raybould over the prosecution of engineering firm SNC-Lavalin, leading to her and Jane Philpott's resignation from cabinet in early 2019 and their later expulsion from the Liberal caucus. Scheer framed the race around affordability, while the Liberals had already revived, on August 22, 2019, a 2005 Scheer speech opposing same-sex marriage, which continued to dog his campaign after it launched.
note: Corrected timing: the Scheer same-sex-marriage video was revived August 22, 2019, before the campaign launched, not 'early in the campaign'.

summary: Cannabis had been legal for recreational use across Canada since October 17, 2018, under the Cannabis Act, making Canada the second country after Uruguay to legalize adult-use cannabis federally; adults could legally possess limited amounts, buy from licensed retailers, and grow a small number of plants at home, subject to provincial rules. Separately, Canada's opioid crisis continued to worsen: federal data released in mid-2019 showed more than 10,300 apparent opioid-related deaths between January 2016 and September 2018, with 4,460 deaths recorded in 2018 alone and fentanyl implicated in roughly three-quarters of them, concentrated in British Columbia, Ontario and Alberta.

Canada-China relations remained severely strained through mid-2019 following the December 1, 2018 arrest in Vancouver of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou on a US extradition request. In apparent retaliation, China detained two Canadians, Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor, in December 2018 and accused them in March 2019 of stealing state secrets; it also blocked canola imports from major Canadian exporters that same month. In May 2019, China's ambassador to Canada said relations were at their lowest point since diplomatic ties began decades earlier. Meanwhile, Canada's steel and aluminum tariff dispute with the United States was resolved in May 2019, and the new USMCA trade deal, signed in November 2018, awaited ratification.

Canada's economy grew modestly through 2019. The Bank of Canada projected real GDP growth of around 1.5% for 2019, citing weaker commodity prices and global trade tensions, and held its key interest rate at 1.75% throughout the year, including at its meetings in May and October. The national unemployment rate stayed low, around 5.5%, and Canada added roughly 320,000 jobs over the year. Housing affordability had deteriorated sharply in 2018, with the national RBC affordability measure reaching its worst level since 1990 before easing slightly late in 2018, then declining again in the first quarter of 2019, keeping cost-of-living concerns, particularly housing, salient heading into the fall election.

Economic policy debates in 2019 centred on trade, taxation and subsidies ahead of the federal election. The Bank of Canada held its key rate at 1.75% through 2019 amid modest GDP growth (around 1.5%) and continuing trade uncertainty from the Canada-US steel and aluminum tariff dispute, resolved only in May 2019, and the yet-unratified USMCA trade deal signed in November 2018. Corporate subsidies and economic development spending were debated in Parliament and on the campaign trail that began September 11, 2019, alongside federal deficit projections following several years of Liberal government deficit spending since 2015.

Health care policy drew national attention in 2019 following the release, on June 12, 2019, of the federal Advisory Council on the Implementation of National Pharmacare's final report, chaired by Eric Hoskins. It recommended a universal, single-payer national pharmacare program covering prescription drugs, administered by provinces but funded and standards-set federally, with essential medicines covered by 2022 and a full formulary by 2027, estimated to save about $5 billion annually. Budget 2019 had already announced $35 million to create a transition office and steps toward a Canadian Drug Agency, making pharmacare a live issue for parties ahead of the fall election campaign.

Climate policy was contentious through 2018-2019. The federal government's carbon pricing plan, starting at $10/tonne in 2019 and rising annually to $50/tonne by 2022, was imposed in April 2019 on four provinces (Ontario, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and New Brunswick) that had refused to adopt their own carbon price, prompting legal challenges. Alberta's new premier, Jason Kenney, elected in April 2019, moved to repeal the province's carbon tax. In February 2019, the "United We Roll" convoy of pipeline and oil-industry supporters travelled from Alberta to Ottawa to protest the carbon tax and environmental-assessment legislation (Bill C-69), drawing both support and criticism. The Trans Mountain pipeline expansion, which Canada purchased for $4.5 billion in 2018, remained under review.

Immigration remained a major issue heading into the fall 2019 election, driven by sustained irregular border crossings into Quebec at Roxham Road, where tens of thousands of asylum seekers had crossed since 2017, producing long processing backlogs at the Immigration and Refugee Board. The federal government had pledged $173 million for border security and faster claims processing and compensated nearby residents. Economic immigration levels also continued to rise under the Liberal government's multi-year immigration plan. The issue was expected to be especially salient in Quebec as parties, including the Bloc Quebecois under new leader Yves-Francois Blanchet, campaigned ahead of the October 21 vote.

Quebec politics was shaped by the secularism debate and a resurgent Bloc Quebecois ahead of the October 2019 election. Premier Francois Legault's government passed Bill 21 on June 16, 2019, banning religious symbols for public employees in positions of authority, after large Montreal protests earlier in the year; the law was challenged in court shortly after passage. Yves- Francois Blanchet became Bloc Quebecois leader in January 2019 and sought to rebuild the party's standing in Quebec for the fall campaign, emphasizing Quebec autonomy, language, and secularism. Debates over bilingualism and the federal government's role in Quebec's jurisdiction continued through the campaign that began September 11, 2019.

The new USMCA (CUSMA) trade agreement, signed by Canada, the US and Mexico in November 2018 and amended in December 2019, was ratified by the US Congress in January 2020 and by Canada's Parliament in March 2020, with implementation expected later in 2020. This followed the resolution in May 2019 of a steel-and-aluminum tariff dispute between Canada and the United States. Trade relations in early 2020 were also affected by the global economic disruption of the emerging COVID-19 pandemic, which Statistics Canada noted had begun reducing trade with China and travel advisories by February 2020, ahead of the broader shutdown that began in March 2020.

Indigenous reconciliation was a major national issue through this period. On June 3, 2019, the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls released its final report, "Reclaiming Power and Place," which concluded that Indigenous women and girls faced disproportionate violence in Canada and issued 231 Calls for Justice; the federal government said it accepted all calls. In February 2020, RCMP enforcement of an injunction against Wet'suwet'en hereditary chiefs opposing the Coastal GasLink pipeline in northern British Columbia triggered weeks of solidarity protests and rail blockades across the country, including in Ontario and Quebec, that disrupted CN Rail and Via Rail service into March 2020.

Gender equality remained a live policy area through this period. Federal pay equity legislation, passed in late 2018, continued moving toward implementation through regulation in 2019 and early 2020. Women's representation in federal politics was debated during and after the October 2019 election, which returned a Liberal minority government. The #MeToo movement's focus on workplace harassment and women's advancement continued to shape public discussion, alongside ongoing debate over abortion access, which became a campaign issue in 2019 when Conservative leader Andrew Scheer said he was personally "pro-life" but would not reopen the abortion debate if elected.

Protest and civil-liberties issues were prominent in this period. In February 2020, RCMP enforcement of an injunction on Wet'suwet'en territory against the Coastal GasLink pipeline sparked weeks of solidarity protests and rail blockades across Canada, including in Ontario and Quebec, disrupting national rail service until early March 2020. Quebec's Bill 21, banning religious symbols for public employees in positions of authority, took effect after passing on June 16, 2019, following large protests, and remained subject to legal challenges into 2020. By March 2020, newly introduced public-health emergency measures in Quebec and other provinces, such as school and business closures to curb COVID-19, raised separate questions about the scope of government emergency powers.

Justin Trudeau's Liberals won re-election on October 21, 2019, but were reduced to a minority government with 157 seats, finishing narrowly ahead of Andrew Scheer's Conservatives (121 seats, and a higher popular-vote share) with the Bloc Quebecois rebounding to 32 seats under new leader Yves-Francois Blanchet, the NDP winning 24 seats, and the Greens 3. The result followed the SNC-Lavalin affair earlier in 2019. Through late 2019 and into early 2020, the minority Parliament required Trudeau's government to negotiate support from opposition parties, and in March-April 2020 the federal government introduced emergency spending measures in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

On April 18-19, 2020, a gunman killed 22 people in and around Portapique, Nova Scotia, in Canada's worst mass shooting, including RCMP Constable Heidi Stevenson; the attacker was shot dead by police. Citing the massacre, the federal government on May 1, 2020 banned more than 1,500 models of assault-style firearms, including the AR-15, by order-in-council, with a two-year amnesty for current owners. Separately, Canada's opioid crisis continued to worsen: federal data showed 4,460 apparent opioid-related deaths in 2018 alone, with fentanyl implicated in roughly three-quarters of them, concentrated in British Columbia, Ontario and Alberta. By spring 2020, public safety enforcement increasingly focused on COVID-19 measures introduced across provinces, including Quebec, starting in March 2020.
note: Added the April 2020 Nova Scotia mass shooting and May 1, 2020 assault-style firearms ban (most salient pre-cutoff event, previously omitted); trimmed sex-work-law filler.

summary: Canada-China relations remained severely strained throughout this period. Following the December 2018 arrest of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou in Vancouver and China's detention of Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor in apparent retaliation, relations stayed tense through 2019, with China's ambassador describing ties as being at "rock bottom" in May 2019; the two detained Canadians remained in Chinese custody into 2020, and Meng's extradition case continued before Canadian courts. Separately, in January 2020, Iran's military shot down Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752 shortly after takeoff from Tehran, killing all 176 people aboard, including 55 Canadian citizens and dozens of permanent residents, prompting a Canadian-led international investigation demanding accountability from Iran.

Cost-of-living and household finances were already a concern before COVID-19 struck. Housing affordability had worsened through 2018 and into 2019 in many Canadian markets, especially Vancouver and Toronto, before the pandemic brought a sudden economic shock: Statistics Canada reported real GDP growth had already slowed to just 0.1% in January 2020 and stalled in February 2020, partly due to reduced trade with China. Quebec declared a public health emergency on March 14, 2020, and ordered non-essential businesses closed starting March 24, 2020, triggering mass layoffs and a sharp rise in applications for federal emergency income support introduced in late March and April 2020.

Canada's economy slowed sharply heading into 2020. After modest growth of around 1.5% in 2019, Statistics Canada reported GDP grew just 0.1% in January 2020 and stalled in February, hurt partly by reduced trade with China and looming US tariff threats. The COVID-19 pandemic then caused an unprecedented economic shock: Quebec ordered non-essential businesses closed from March 24, 2020, and similar shutdowns occurred across Canada, leading to mass layoffs. The federal government responded with large-scale emergency spending, including the Canada Emergency Response Benefit introduced in late March 2020, and businesses sought government loans and wage subsidies amid the abrupt halt in economic activity.

COVID-19 reached Quebec in late February 2020, with the first confirmed case on February 27 in a Montreal-area resident who had travelled from Iran. As cases rose, Premier Francois Legault banned large indoor gatherings on March 12, closed schools, daycares and universities on March 13, and declared a public health emergency on March 14, asking those over 70 to stay home. On March 23, Legault ordered all non-essential businesses closed starting March 24, and Montreal declared a state of emergency on March 27 as cases approached 1,000. By mid-April 2020, Quebec had become Canada's hardest-hit province, with lockdown measures continuing and the federal government rolling out emergency income and business support programs.

Climate and energy policy remained contentious through this period. The federal carbon tax, applied since April 2019 to provinces without their own equivalent pricing, continued to face legal challenges from Saskatchewan, Ontario and Alberta, whose premier Jason Kenney had repealed the province's own carbon levy after taking office in 2019. The "United We Roll" pro-pipeline convoy protested the carbon tax and environmental-assessment law in Ottawa in February 2019. In February 2020, opposition to the Coastal GasLink pipeline through Wet'suwet'en territory in British Columbia triggered nationwide rail blockades lasting several weeks, renewing debate over energy infrastructure, Indigenous rights and climate policy.

Immigration remained a significant policy area through 2019 and into early 2020. Irregular border crossings at Roxham Road in Quebec continued, with thousands more asylum seekers intercepted in 2019, adding to a multi-year backlog of refugee claims. Immigration policy was debated during the October 2019 federal election, after which Trudeau's Liberals formed a minority government. By March 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic began to affect immigration directly, as Canada restricted international travel and border crossings in mid-March 2020, with exemptions initially allowing some cross-border movement before broader restrictions tightened.

Quebec politics continued to centre on identity and language issues through this period. Bill 21, Quebec's secularism law banning religious symbols for public employees in positions of authority, took effect after passing on June 16, 2019, and remained the subject of ongoing court challenges into 2020. The Bloc Quebecois, led by Yves-Francois Blanchet since January 2019, rebounded to 32 seats in the October 2019 federal election, emphasizing Quebec autonomy and language protections. From March 2020, Quebec's COVID-19 response, including a public health emergency declared March 14 and a non-essential business closure from March 24, became a dominant feature of the provincial government's relationship with Ottawa and other provinces.

Joe Biden became U.S. president on January 20, 2021 and, that same day, cancelled the permit for the Keystone XL pipeline, a project Canada had supported. Biden and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau held a virtual bilateral meeting on February 23, 2021, unveiling a "Roadmap for a Renewed Canada-U.S. Partnership" pledging cooperation on the pandemic, climate change and the economy. Canada and the U.S. also kept their shared land border closed to non-essential travel throughout this period, with restrictions extended monthly since March 2020, most recently through May 21, 2021. A long-running U.S.-Canada softwood lumber dispute continued unresolved, with combined duties on Canadian lumber reduced to about 8.99% following a December 2020 review.
note: Removed claim that Washington had already 'proposed to raise' lumber duties again: that preliminary announcement came May 21, 2021, the day after the cutoff; added border-closure renewal date and precise roadmap name.

summary: Reconciliation with Indigenous peoples remained a prominent issue in Canada through early 2021, following the 2015 Truth and Reconciliation Commission's calls to action and continued attention to the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls inquiry (2019). The federal government faced ongoing criticism for slow progress on long-term boil-water advisories on reserves and on implementing the TRC's recommendations. Legal and political disputes over Indigenous land and resource rights, including pipeline-related disputes such as the Wet'suwet'en opposition to the Coastal GasLink pipeline in 2020, continued to draw national attention. As of this date, the mass unmarked-grave discoveries at former residential schools that would dominate national debate had not yet occurred.

Gender equality remained a federal policy focus: Ottawa had created a dedicated Department for Women and Gender Equality and continued work toward proactive pay-equity legislation for federally regulated workplaces. The COVID-19 pandemic disproportionately affected women's employment, with commentators describing a 'she-cession' as women left the workforce in greater numbers than men during 2020. The government had also amended the Criminal Code and the Canadian Human Rights Act to add protections based on gender identity and expression. Discrimination against racialized Canadians also drew national attention following the summer 2020 Black Lives Matter protests across Canadian cities.

Canada's minority Liberal government, re-elected in October 2019, continued to rely on opposition support in the House of Commons through the pandemic, fueling speculation about an early election. Several provinces, including British Columbia and Saskatchewan, held elections in 2020 that relied heavily on expanded vote-by-mail options because of COVID-19, with turnout and counting procedures adapted accordingly. No federal election had yet been called as of this date; Elections Canada had nonetheless prepared contingency plans for an eventual pandemic-era federal vote, including expanded mail-in ballot capacity.

Justin Trudeau's Liberals governed with a minority in the House of Commons following the October 2019 election. In August 2020, Finance Minister Bill Morneau resigned amid the WE Charity controversy, a conflict-of-interest matter over a sole-sourced student-grant program; Chrystia Freeland succeeded him as Canada's first female finance minister. On May 13, 2021, federal ethics commissioner Mario Dion cleared Trudeau of wrongdoing in the WE Charity affair but found that Morneau had violated conflict-of-interest rules. The government tabled its first pandemic-era federal budget on April 19, 2021, proposing roughly $101 billion in new spending, including a national child-care plan, after posting a $354.2 billion deficit for fiscal year 2020-21.

Canada-China relations remained severely strained. Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou had been arrested in Vancouver in December 2018 on a U.S. extradition request, and China responded by detaining Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor on espionage allegations. In March 2021, Chinese courts tried both men on espionage-related charges in closed-door proceedings, but as of this date no verdicts had been announced. Meng's extradition hearings continued in Canadian courts through this period, with no resolution reached, and the so-called 'two Michaels' remained detained in China as of this date.
note: Removed Aug 2021 Spavor sentencing (occurred after the May 20, 2021 cutoff); reworded to reflect that verdicts were still pending.

summary: Canada experienced successive COVID-19 waves through 2020-21, with provinces such as Ontario and Quebec imposing lockdowns, curfews and business closures, including a record case surge in Ontario in December 2020. Health Canada authorized the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine in early December 2020, and vaccinations began on December 14, 2020, reaching all provinces by mid-January 2021. The rollout was initially slow: by late March 2021 only about 7% of Canadians had received one dose, well behind the United States. More contagious variants (including the Alpha variant) drove a third wave of infections in spring 2021, prompting renewed restrictions in several provinces, including Ontario's stay-at-home order issued in April 2021.

Canada's federal carbon tax, part of the Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act, took effect in provinces without equivalent provincial pricing starting in 2019, rising annually; several provinces challenged it in court. On March 25, 2021, the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the law's constitutionality in a 6-3 ruling. In December 2020, Ottawa unveiled a strengthened climate plan, 'A Healthy Environment and a Healthy Economy,' including about $15 billion for measures such as a Clean Electricity Standard and a schedule of carbon-price increases reaching $170 per tonne by 2030. Legislation to enshrine a 2050 net-zero emissions target in law was before Parliament during this period.

The irregular border crossing at Roxham Road, Quebec, a major entry point for asylum seekers from the United States, had been closed by the federal government in March 2020 due to the pandemic, and remained closed as of this date, sharply reducing irregular crossings that had numbered in the tens of thousands annually before 2020. Canada's overall immigration levels fell substantially in 2020 because of pandemic travel restrictions, prompting Ottawa to raise its 2021-2023 immigration targets to around 400,000 newcomers per year to compensate.

Quebec's Bill 21, adopted in June 2019, bars some public employees in positions of authority (such as teachers, police officers and judges) from wearing religious symbols at work, invoking the notwithstanding clause to shield it from Charter challenges; litigation continued, and on April 20, 2021 the Quebec Superior Court struck down parts of the law as it applied to English-language school boards and to members of the legislature. On May 13, 2021, Premier Francois Legault's government tabled Bill 96, a major reform of the French-language charter (Bill 101) meant to reinforce French as Quebec's common and official language, proposing to again invoke the notwithstanding clause and to expand francization requirements for businesses.
note: Corrected timing error: Bill 96 was tabled May 13, 2021, before the May 20, 2021 cutoff, not 'not yet introduced.'

summary: Joe Biden became U.S. president on January 20, 2021 and that day cancelled the Keystone XL pipeline permit, a project Canada had backed. Biden and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau held a virtual bilateral meeting on February 23, 2021, pledging cooperation on the pandemic, climate and the economy. Canada and the U.S. kept their shared land border closed to non-essential travel from March 2020 onward, extending the closure monthly; it remained closed as of this date even as Canada began reopening to some fully vaccinated travelers in summer 2021. A long-running softwood lumber dispute also continued, with the U.S. Commerce Department proposing on May 21, 2021 to roughly double duties on Canadian lumber imports.

On May 27, 2021, the Tk'emlups te Secwepemc First Nation announced that ground-penetrating radar had found what were believed to be 215 unmarked graves at the site of the former Kamloops Indian Residential School in British Columbia. The discovery prompted national mourning; Prime Minister Justin Trudeau ordered flags on federal buildings lowered to half-mast, and similar searches were launched at other former residential-school sites across the country, including one at the former Marieval school in Saskatchewan where the Cowessess First Nation announced on June 23, 2021 that it had located as many as 751 unmarked graves. The events intensified national debate over reconciliation and the legacy of the residential school system, which operated with federal and church involvement for over a century.

Gender equality remained a federal policy focus: Ottawa had created a dedicated Department for Women and Gender Equality, and the federal Pay Equity Act, passed in 2018, was set to come into force on August 31, 2021, requiring federally regulated employers to establish proactive pay-equity plans. The pandemic disproportionately affected women's employment through 2020-21, a pattern commentators called a 'she-cession.' Discrimination against racialized Canadians drew sustained national attention following the summer 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, and the Kamloops residential-school grave discovery of May 2021 intensified public discussion of discrimination against Indigenous peoples. Canada ranked 24th of 156 countries in the World Economic Forum's 2021 Global Gender Gap Report.
note: Pay Equity Act regulations did not take effect until Aug 31, 2021, after the Aug 17 cutoff; changed 'continued implementation' to 'set to come into force.'

summary: Public-health restrictions imposed across Canada during the COVID-19 pandemic, including curfews, business closures, gathering limits and, from spring 2021, vaccine-passport discussions in some provinces, prompted recurring protests over personal freedoms. Demonstrations against masks and lockdowns occurred in multiple cities from 2020 onward, including a large anti-lockdown march in Montreal on March 13, 2021, and periodic rallies in Vancouver, Calgary and other cities. Separately, Quebec's Bill 21 on religious symbols and ongoing debates over hate speech and online harms kept questions about the balance between free expression, religious freedom and protection from discrimination in the public debate.

Prime Minister Justin Trudeau called a federal election on August 15, 2021, asking the Governor General to dissolve Parliament roughly two years into his minority government, with a vote to follow in September. Elections Canada expanded mail-in voting options because of the pandemic; more than a million Canadians had requested special mail-in ballot kits by mid-August 2021, and officials said counting of mail ballots would not begin until after polls closed. Earlier pandemic-era provincial elections, including British Columbia's and Saskatchewan's in 2020, had already relied heavily on expanded vote-by-mail procedures.

Justin Trudeau's Liberals governed with a minority since October 2019. Finance Minister Bill Morneau resigned in August 2020 amid the WE Charity conflict-of-interest controversy and was succeeded by Chrystia Freeland. On May 13, 2021, the federal ethics commissioner cleared Trudeau of wrongdoing in that affair while finding Morneau had breached conflict-of-interest rules. Ottawa tabled a pandemic recovery budget on April 19, 2021 with about $101 billion in new spending, after a $354.2 billion deficit in fiscal 2020-21. On August 15, 2021, Trudeau called a federal election, seeking a majority mandate roughly two years into his minority government.

Canada legalized recreational cannabis in October 2018, and by this period possession within legal limits was no longer a criminal offence. On April 30, 2020, following the April 2020 Nova Scotia mass shooting that killed 22 people, the federal government banned more than 1,500 models of 'assault-style' firearms by order-in-council, Canada's largest one-time gun ban, while also announcing plans for further legislation on handguns and buybacks. A Statistics Canada report on 2020 police-reported crime, released in July 2021, counted 8,344 victims of a crime involving a firearm that year, about 2.8% of all violent-crime victims.
note: Replaced a firearm-rate statistic from a May 2022 StatCan report (not yet published as of the Aug 17, 2021 cutoff) with the comparable figure from the July 2021 report.

summary: Canada-China relations remained severely strained over the case of Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou, arrested in Vancouver in December 2018 on a U.S. extradition request, and the retaliatory detention of Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor in China on espionage allegations. In March 2021, Chinese courts tried both men; Spavor was sentenced in August 2021 to 11 years in prison, while a verdict in Kovrig's case remained pending as of this date. Meng's extradition hearings continued in a Canadian court through 2021 without resolution.

Canada's annual inflation rate rose through 2021, reaching 3.6% in May and continuing upward over the summer, driven by rebounding energy prices, supply-chain bottlenecks and a low base from 2020. Housing costs rose sharply: average home prices nationwide increased by more than 20% year-over-year during 2021, which commentators linked to low interest rates and strong demand. The Bank of Canada held its key policy rate at a record-low 0.25% throughout this period to support the pandemic recovery, even as price pressures built.

The federal government posted a $354.2 billion deficit for fiscal year 2020-21, driven by large-scale pandemic income supports and business subsidies such as the Canada Emergency Response Benefit and wage subsidy programs. On April 19, 2021, Ottawa tabled its first pandemic-era budget, proposing about $101 billion in further new spending over several years, including a national child-care plan and green investment programs, with the deficit projected to fall to $154.7 billion in 2021-22. Canada's economy was recovering unevenly through 2021 as provinces lifted and reimposed public-health restrictions amid successive COVID-19 waves.

The COVID-19 pandemic placed severe strain on Canada's health care system. A Fraser Institute report found Canadians faced a median wait of 22.6 weeks for medically necessary treatment in 2020, the longest wait on record and up sharply from 9.3 weeks in 1993. A Canadian Institute for Health Information report published June 15, 2021 on the pandemic's first six months found reduced volumes for priority procedures such as hip and knee replacements and cataract surgery compared with pre-pandemic levels. Long-term care homes were especially hard-hit: roughly 80% of Canada's COVID-19 deaths in the pandemic's first wave occurred among long-term care residents, prompting federal and provincial reviews of staffing levels, infection control and facility standards in the sector.
note: The '560,000 fewer surgeries' figure came from a CIHI report published Dec 9, 2021, after the Aug 17, 2021 cutoff; replaced with data available by the cutoff and corrected source attribution for the 22.6-week figure.

summary: Canada experienced successive COVID-19 waves through 2020-21, with provinces including Ontario and Quebec imposing lockdowns and curfews, notably during a severe third wave in spring 2021 driven by variants such as Alpha and, later, Delta. Vaccinations began December 14, 2020 and expanded through 2021 after a slow start; by summer 2021 Canada had among the highest vaccination rates in the world, and provinces progressively lifted restrictions. Prime Minister Trudeau called a federal election on August 15, 2021, with public-health measures, including masking and distancing at campaign events and expanded mail-in voting, remaining in place because the pandemic was ongoing.

Canada's federal carbon tax, under the Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act, continued to rise on a preset schedule; the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the law's constitutionality on March 25, 2021. In December 2020, Ottawa had unveiled a strengthened climate plan including roughly $15 billion for measures such as a Clean Electricity Standard, and a schedule raising the carbon price to $170 per tonne by 2030. On June 29, 2021, the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act became law, legally committing Canada to net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 and setting a 2030 target of 40-45% below 2005 levels.

The irregular border crossing at Roxham Road, Quebec, a major entry point for asylum seekers from the United States, had been closed since March 2020 due to the pandemic and remained closed as of this date, sharply curtailing irregular crossings that previously numbered in the tens of thousands annually. Pandemic travel restrictions had reduced overall immigration levels in 2020, prompting Ottawa to raise its immigration targets for 2021-2023 to around 400,000 newcomers per year. Canada also continued to welcome Afghan nationals who had worked with Canadian forces, with resettlement efforts intensifying as the security situation in Afghanistan deteriorated in mid-2021.

Quebec's Bill 21 (2019) bars some public employees in positions of authority, such as teachers, police officers and judges, from wearing religious symbols at work, protected from Charter challenge by the notwithstanding clause. On April 20, 2021, the Quebec Superior Court struck down parts of the law as applied to English-language school boards and to members of the legislature; appeals continued. On May 13, 2021, Premier François Legault's government tabled Bill 96, a major reform of the French-language charter (Bill 101) that makes French Quebec's sole official and common language, caps English CEGEP enrolment, pre-emptively invokes the notwithstanding clause and proposes amending Canada's Constitution to recognize Quebec as a nation.

Canada and the United States remained each other's top trading partners under CUSMA, but several irritants persisted. In July 2021 Canada's trade minister raised concerns with the US Trade Representative over the proposed Buy America procurement rules. The US Commerce Department's 2021 review proposed raising softwood lumber duties on Canadian exports to a combined average of 18.32%, part of a dispute that had cost Canadian producers over $8 billion in tariffs since 2017; Ottawa created a relief fund for affected companies in early 2022. Other frictions included US tariffs on Canadian solar products and continued operation of the Line 5 pipeline, while both countries stressed keeping cross-border supply chains open.

In May 2021, ground-penetrating radar at the former Kamloops Indian Residential School site revealed an estimated 215 unmarked graves of children, a discovery that prompted national mourning and renewed attention to Canada's residential school system, which separated roughly 150,000 Indigenous children from their families. The following month, Cowessess First Nation in Saskatchewan announced the discovery of 751 unmarked graves near the former Marieval Indian Residential School, and about 160 more were found at the site of the former Kuper Island Residential School in British Columbia. Canada observed its first National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on September 30, 2021. Canadian Press editors named the Kamloops discovery the top news story of 2021.

Following the September 2021 federal election, 103 women held seats in the 338-member House of Commons (30.5%). In the cabinet sworn in on October 26, 2021, 19 of 38 ministers were women, continuing the gender parity in cabinet maintained since 2015; roughly 49% of Senate seats were also held by women. Statistics Canada figures from 2020 showed women earning an average of 89 cents for every dollar earned by men, with the gap larger for Indigenous and immigrant women. On May 2, 2022, Politico published a leaked draft opinion of the US Supreme Court indicating a majority intended to overturn Roe v. Wade, prompting Canadian federal ministers, including the Minister for Women and Gender Equality, to publicly restate commitments to abortion rights.
note: Corrected cabinet gender figure: the 48.6%-women cabinet was the pre-election (July 2021) cabinet; the cabinet sworn in after the election (Oct 26, 2021) was 50% women (19 of 38).

summary: A convoy of truckers and other protesters opposed to COVID-19 vaccine mandates, organized after a January 15, 2022 federal requirement that cross-border truckers be vaccinated, arrived in Ottawa in late January 2022 and occupied streets around Parliament Hill for weeks. Related blockades closed border crossings, including the Ambassador Bridge between Windsor and Detroit. On February 14, 2022, the federal government invoked the Emergencies Act for the first time since its creation, granting powers including the freezing of protesters' bank accounts and designation of no-go zones; the declaration was revoked on February 23, 2022, after police cleared the demonstrations.

In the September 20, 2021 federal election, a record 1.2 million Canadians requested mail-in ballots, though Elections Canada later reported that nearly 100,000 were not counted, mostly for arriving after the deadline. A 2021 government bill to expand weekend voting and mail-in ballot access did not pass before the snap election was called. After the Liberal-NDP confidence-and-supply agreement of March 2022, the parties committed to pursuing electoral reforms such as extending polling-station hours and allowing voting at any polling place within one's electoral district.

In the September 20, 2021 federal election, Justin Trudeau's Liberals won a third consecutive minority government, with about 160 of 338 seats, against 119 for the Conservatives, 32 for the Bloc Quebecois, 25 for the NDP and 2 for the Greens. In March 2022, the Liberals and NDP signed a confidence-and-supply agreement under which the NDP agreed to support the government on budgets and confidence votes in exchange for policy commitments. On February 2, 2022, Conservative leader Erin O'Toole was removed by his own caucus in a 73-45 vote; Pierre Poilievre declared his candidacy for the leadership on February 5, 2022, with the vote to choose a new leader still pending.

On September 24, 2021, China released Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor, who had been detained since December 2018, the same day Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou reached a deal with US prosecutors and returned to China, easing one major source of tension in Canada-China relations. Russia invaded Ukraine on February 24, 2022; Canada responded with sanctions against Russian officials and entities and announced military and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine. Through early April 2022, Canadian and Chinese foreign ministers exchanged views on the war, with Canada's Melanie Joly saying Canada would announce further sanctions against Russia.

Canadian inflation accelerated through late 2021 and early 2022. The annual pace reached 4.7% in October 2021, the fastest increase in 18 years, driven partly by rising housing, grocery and gasoline prices; average home prices nationally rose more than 25% in 2021. In March 2022, the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by 25 basis points, its first increase in over two years, and followed with a further hike in April 2022, moving the rate up from a pandemic-era low of 0.25%. Analysts anticipated additional rate increases as the Bank sought to bring inflation, which continued to run well above its 2% target, back under control.

Canada experienced a large Omicron-variant COVID-19 wave over the winter of 2021-2022. On January 15, 2022, a federal requirement took effect that cross-border truck drivers be vaccinated to avoid quarantine on entry. Opposition to this and other public health measures fueled the 'Freedom Convoy,' which arrived in Ottawa in late January 2022 and occupied the area around Parliament for weeks, while related blockades closed border crossings such as the Ambassador Bridge. On February 14, 2022, the federal government invoked the Emergencies Act to end the protests and blockades, revoking it on February 23 after police cleared the sites.

In June 2021, Canada's Parliament passed the Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act, legally committing the country to net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 through five-year interim targets, and adopted an enhanced 2030 target of cutting emissions 40-45% below 2005 levels. At the COP26 summit in Glasgow in November 2021, Prime Minister Trudeau pledged to cap and reduce oil and gas sector emissions, cut oil and gas methane emissions by at least 75% below 2012 levels by 2030, work toward ending thermal coal exports by 2030, and achieve a net-zero electricity grid by 2035. On March 29, 2022, the federal government released its 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan, the first plan issued under the Net-Zero Act, including about $9.1 billion in new investments and a mandate for zero-emission vehicles to reach 100% of new light-duty vehicle sales by 2035.
note: The 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan was actually released March 29, 2022 (before the May 6, 2022 cutoff); corrected from 'committed to table by end of March 2022' to the dated fact of its release and content.

summary: Following the Taliban's takeover of Afghanistan in August 2021, Canada pledged to resettle Afghan refugees, including many who arrived via irregular routes. The irregular border crossing at Roxham Road, Quebec, which had been closed since the pandemic began in March 2020, reopened in November 2021, and crossings increased through early 2022, prompting federal projections of up to 50,000 irregular asylum claims for the year, around 95% of them in Quebec. In February 2022, Canada's Immigration Levels Plan raised the admission target to 431,645 permanent residents for 2022, part of a broader plan to increase annual intake in subsequent years.

Quebec's Bill 96, tabled in May 2021 by Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette, proposed a major overhaul of the Charter of the French Language, aiming to make French the sole common language of Quebec, extend language rules to businesses with 25 or more employees, cap enrolment at English-language junior colleges (CEGEPs), and create a new Commissioner of the French Language. Committee hearings in fall 2021 heard from 51 witnesses, including Indigenous and anglophone groups who raised concerns. Clause-by-clause study resumed in 2022; by February about a quarter of the bill's 201 articles had been reviewed, and a further amended report was tabled April 26, 2022. The bill remained before the National Assembly, with the minister seeking its adoption in the coming weeks.

US President Joe Biden made his first visit to Canada as president on March 23-24, 2023, meeting Prime Minister Trudeau and addressing a joint session of Parliament. Trade irritants persisted alongside the visit: the US formally disputed Canada's dairy quota allocations under CUSMA in early 2023, and softwood lumber duties remained unresolved, having cost Canadian exporters more than $8 billion since 2017. During Biden's visit, the two leaders announced an agreement, effective March 25, 2023, expanding the Safe Third Country Agreement to cover the entire Canada-US border, allowing Canada to close the Roxham Road irregular crossing in Quebec.

Pope Francis traveled to Canada from July 24 to 29, 2022, on what he called a 'penitential pilgrimage,' apologizing on Canadian soil in Maskwacis, Alberta, Quebec City and Iqaluit for the Catholic Church's role in the residential school system, in which more than 150,000 Indigenous children were separated from their families and at least 4,000 died from neglect or abuse. The visit followed the May 2021 discovery of 215 unmarked graves at the former Kamloops Indian Residential School and subsequent findings at other former school sites across the country. Canada observed its second National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on September 30, 2022.

On June 24, 2022, the US Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, ending the constitutional right to abortion in the United States. Prime Minister Trudeau and Women and Gender Equality Minister Marci Ien publicly reaffirmed Canada's commitment to abortion access, while hundreds of people protested outside the Montreal courthouse in solidarity with Americans affected by the ruling; an anti-abortion group active in Conservative Party circles welcomed the decision. Federal budgets in this period continued to include gender-based budgeting analysis, and Statistics Canada data showed continued, gradual increases in the share of women in Parliament and on federal courts.

The Public Order Emergency Commission, led by Justice Paul Rouleau, examined the federal government's February 2022 invocation of the Emergencies Act to end the 'Freedom Convoy' protests against COVID-19 measures, which had occupied downtown Ottawa and blocked border crossings. Its report, released February 17, 2023, concluded that the legal threshold for invoking the Act had been met, while criticizing specific measures such as the freezing of protesters' bank accounts and the lack of a clear mechanism to unfreeze them; the commission made 56 recommendations, including changes to the Act itself. Convoy-related protests recurred in Ottawa around the anniversary in early 2023.

Beginning in February 2023, Global News and the Globe and Mail published reports, based on leaked Canadian Security Intelligence Service material, alleging that China's government had attempted to interfere in Canada's 2019 and 2021 federal elections, including through undisclosed financial support for preferred candidates. The reports prompted opposition parties to demand a public inquiry. In March 2023, Prime Minister Trudeau appointed former governor general David Johnston as an independent special rapporteur to examine the allegations and recommend whether a formal inquiry was warranted.

Pierre Poilievre won the Conservative Party of Canada leadership decisively on September 10, 2022, taking 68.15% of points on the first ballot. The Liberal minority government, led by Justin Trudeau, continued to rely on its March 2022 confidence-and-supply agreement with the NDP, under which the NDP supports the government on budget and confidence votes until 2025 in exchange for policy commitments. The federal budget tabled on March 28, 2023, expanded the new Canadian Dental Care Plan to additional groups and included other cost-of-living measures, as part of continuing to implement the Liberal-NDP agreement.

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched February 24, 2022, continued through this period; Canada provided ongoing military, financial and humanitarian support to Ukraine, including further funding pledges announced by Defence Minister Anita Anand. Canada-China relations remained tense following reports, from February 2023 onward, that Canadian intelligence had assessed Chinese government interference in Canada's 2019 and 2021 federal elections; Prime Minister Trudeau appointed David Johnston as independent special rapporteur on foreign interference in March 2023. Earlier, at the November 2022 G20 summit in Bali, Chinese President Xi Jinping publicly confronted Trudeau over a leaked account of their conversation.

Canadian inflation remained elevated through 2022 and into early 2023. Annual CPI inflation reached 6.8% in May 2022, the highest since January 1991, then 6.9% in September, before easing to 6.3% in December 2022 and 5.9% in January 2023; grocery prices rose particularly sharply throughout the period. In response, the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate repeatedly over 2022, a cumulative increase of about 400 basis points, bringing the rate to 4.25%. Rising living costs contributed to increased demand at food banks, including a 33% rise in visits to the Ottawa Food Bank compared with pre-pandemic levels.

Canada continued implementing its 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan, tabled in March 2022, which set a target of cutting greenhouse gas emissions 40-45% below 2005 levels by 2030 and included a planned cap on oil and gas sector emissions. Construction continued on the federally owned Trans Mountain pipeline expansion, which faced cost overruns and construction delays. Environment Minister Steven Guilbeault continued to signal that regulations capping oil and gas emissions were forthcoming, with the cap expected to begin applying later in the decade. Canada had also pledged at COP26 in 2021 to work toward a net-zero electricity grid by 2035.

Irregular border crossings into Quebec at Roxham Road reached a record of roughly 39,000 in 2022, becoming a major point of federal-provincial tension, with Quebec Premier Francois Legault asking Ottawa to close the crossing. In November 2022, Canada's Immigration Levels Plan raised admission targets to 465,000 permanent residents for 2023, 485,000 for 2024 and 500,000 for 2025. On March 24, 2023, following talks between Prime Minister Trudeau and President Biden, Canada and the United States announced an agreement expanding the Safe Third Country Agreement across the entire shared border, enabling the closure of the Roxham Road crossing.

Quebec's National Assembly adopted Bill 96, overhauling the Charter of the French Language, on May 24, 2022, and it received royal assent on June 1, 2022. The law made French the sole language of communication between Quebecers and provincial institutions, extended language rules to smaller businesses, and capped enrolment at English-language CEGEPs. It drew criticism from anglophone, Indigenous and immigrant groups. Legal challenges followed: on August 12, 2022, the Superior Court of Quebec stayed two provisions requiring certified French translations of legal pleadings, and the English Montreal School Board voted to launch its own court challenge to the law.

Canada remained the top destination for US goods exports and a major source of US imports through 2023 and early 2024. The long-running Canada-US softwood lumber dispute continued unresolved. Provincial premiers voiced concern about preserving trade ties as the November 2024 US presidential election approached, given uncertainty over future trade policy. Canada and the US also worked together on critical minerals and electric-vehicle supply chains under the USMCA framework, with a formal review of that trade agreement scheduled for 2026.

Reconciliation efforts continued through 2023-2024. Kimberly Murray, Canada's Independent Special Interlocutor for Missing Children and Unmarked Graves, kept working with Survivors and First Nations communities on a federal legal framework for unmarked burial sites at former residential schools. By March 31, 2024, the Residential Schools Missing Children Community Support Fund had distributed over $216 million to Indigenous communities and organizations. In March 2024, a BC First Nation and the Catholic Church announced a 'sacred covenant' on reconciliation. September 30, 2023 marked the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

Gender equality and reproductive rights were debated through 2023-2024, partly in the shadow of the 2022 US Supreme Court reversal of Roe v. Wade, which fed advocacy warning that Canada was not immune to erosion of abortion access. The federal budget tabled April 16, 2024 included funding for free contraception coverage and additional $10-a-day child care spaces. On February 8, 2024, the Canadian Bar Association passed a resolution committing to oppose any restriction of abortion rights in Canada. Advocacy coalitions called on federal parties to commit to a national action plan against violence targeting women and gender-diverse people.

In late January 2024, demonstrators marked the two-year anniversary of the 2022 'Freedom Convoy' with a rally on Parliament Hill that passed without major incident. In January 2024, Federal Court Justice Richard Mosley ruled that the government's 2022 invocation of the Emergencies Act to end the convoy protests was unreasonable and had violated Charter-protected freedom of expression; the federal government said it would appeal. In late April and early May 2024, pro-Palestinian protest encampments began appearing on Canadian university campuses, including at McGill University in Montreal, the University of Toronto, the University of Ottawa and the University of British Columbia.

A federal Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference, chaired by Quebec Court of Appeal Justice Marie-Josee Hogue, was launched in September 2023 to examine alleged interference by China, Russia and other foreign states in Canada's 2019 and 2021 federal elections. Public hearings began in January 2024. The inquiry's first report, released by the end of February 2024, found that foreign interference did not change the outcome of those elections but had undermined voters' rights and eroded public trust in the process; a final report was due by the end of 2024.

In March 2024, the House of Commons defeated, by a vote of 204-116, a Conservative non-confidence motion tied to the scheduled April 1 increase in the federal carbon price, with Pierre Poilievre's Conservatives pressing the government over the levy. The federal budget was tabled on April 16, 2024 by Finance Minister Chrystia Freeland, and Canada's Housing Plan, aimed at building 3.87 million homes by 2031, was unveiled on April 12, 2024. Justin Trudeau continued to lead a Liberal minority government reliant on support from other parties in the Commons.

Canada expelled Chinese diplomat Zhao Wei from the Toronto consulate in May 2023 amid allegations of interference targeting a Canadian MP. Tensions with China over alleged election interference continued through the Hogue inquiry hearings that began in September 2023 and continued into 2024. On the Russia-Ukraine war, which entered its third year in February 2024, Prime Minister Trudeau traveled to Kyiv and signed a new bilateral security agreement with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, pledging $320 million in additional military assistance plus funding for demining and intelligence-gathering support, as Canada continued to coordinate with allies on sanctions against Russia.

Canadian inflation, which had peaked near 8.1% in mid-2022, eased over the course of 2023, with the consumer price index rising 3.9% for the year overall -- still the largest annual increase since 1991 outside of 2022. The Bank of Canada held its key policy rate at 5%, a 22-year high, from July 2023 through the period, as it worked to bring inflation back to its 1-3% target range. High borrowing costs kept squeezing households, with the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation flagging that roughly 2.2 million Canadian mortgages were due to renew at sharply higher rates over the following two years.

2023 was Canada's worst wildfire season on record, with roughly 16 million hectares burned and smoke blanketing cities across Canada and the northeastern United States through the summer. The federal government pointed to the fires as evidence of the need for climate action, including its consumer carbon price, which rose from $65 to $80 per tonne on April 1, 2024. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre campaigned against the increase and, in March 2024, brought a non-confidence motion over the carbon tax that was defeated in the House of Commons.

Immigration and population growth became prominent policy issues through 2023-2024, as Canada's non-permanent resident population (temporary workers, international students and asylum claimants) grew rapidly, reaching over 2.5 million. In March 2024, the federal government announced a plan to reduce temporary residents from about 6.5% to 5% of the national population over three years. The government also signalled plans to cut the number of new international study permits, from 509,390 approved in 2023 toward a lower target for 2025, citing pressure on housing and public services.

Quebec's reform of its French-language law, Bill 96, which was adopted in May 2022 and took effect that June, continued to be implemented and challenged through 2023-2024, including new French-language requirements affecting federally regulated businesses such as banks and telecoms, and rules affecting access to English-language CEGEPs. English-language school boards and civil-liberties groups pursued legal challenges to several of the law's provisions. At the federal level, Bill C-13, modernizing the Official Languages Act and recognizing Quebec's Charter of the French Language, received royal assent on June 20, 2023.

After Donald Trump's re-election as US president in November 2024 and his inauguration on January 20, 2025, he repeatedly said Canada should become the 51st US state and referred to Justin Trudeau as its 'Governor.' On February 1, 2025, Trump signed an order imposing 25% tariffs on most Canadian goods (10% on energy), which took effect February 4 before a one-month pause after Canada announced border-security measures. On March 4, 2025, the tariffs went into effect; Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs on US goods. Trump also announced 25% tariffs on steel and aluminum imports, effective March 12, 2025.

Debate over diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policy intensified in Canada following US President Trump's January 2025 executive order terminating federal DEI programs in the United States, which fueled similar debate about DEI initiatives at Canadian universities and in the federal public service. A 2024 federal study found that racialized people, Indigenous people and other groups continued to disproportionately report discrimination and unfair treatment. A proposed class action on behalf of current and former Black federal civil servants, alleging racial discrimination in career advancement, continued to work through the courts.

In late April and May 2024, pro-Palestinian protest encampments appeared on university campuses across Canada, including McGill University, the University of Toronto, the University of Ottawa, the University of British Columbia and the University of Alberta, with demonstrators demanding that institutions divest from companies tied to Israel. Quebec Premier Francois Legault and McGill's administration sought police intervention to dismantle the McGill encampment, and courts were asked to order its removal; encampments elsewhere were cleared by police or voluntarily dismantled over the following months.

The federal Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference, led by Justice Marie-Josee Hogue, released its final report on January 28, 2025. It concluded that while the conduct of some unnamed parliamentarians had been troubling, there was no evidence any MP had conspired with a foreign state against Canada's interests; it documented several instances of suspected interference, including by China, Russia, Pakistan and India, and issued 51 recommendations to strengthen election security, about half of which could be implemented before the next general election. In 2024, the Liberals lost byelections in previously safe seats in Toronto-St. Paul's (June) and LaSalle-Emard-Verdun (September). On March 23, 2025, Carney asked the Governor General to dissolve Parliament, calling a federal election for April 28, 2025.

Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Chrystia Freeland resigned from cabinet on December 16, 2024. On January 6, 2025, Justin Trudeau announced he would resign as Liberal leader and prime minister once a successor was chosen, and Parliament was prorogued. A Liberal leadership race ran from late January through early March 2025, with candidates including Mark Carney, Chrystia Freeland and Karina Gould. Mark Carney, former governor of the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England, won on the first ballot on March 9, 2025 with 85.88% of points, and was sworn in as Canada's 24th prime minister on March 14, 2025. Pierre Poilievre remained Conservative leader, Jagmeet Singh led the NDP, and Yves-Francois Blanchet led the Bloc Quebecois. On March 23, 2025, Carney asked the Governor General to dissolve Parliament, calling a federal election for April 28, 2025.

Record levels of auto theft prompted a federal National Summit on Combatting Auto Theft in Ottawa on February 8, 2024, where federal, provincial, municipal, industry and law-enforcement representatives endorsed a statement of intent to fight the problem; vehicle thefts had reached roughly 70,000 in 2023, with carjackings also rising sharply in some regions. Separately, political support for supervised drug-consumption sites weakened in several provinces through 2024: Ontario moved to close about ten sites by the following March in favour of new 'treatment hubs,' and Alberta prepared to close some of its sites. Health Canada's 'safer supply' funding, provided since 2020 through the Substance Use and Addictions Program, was due to expire on March 31, 2025, with no renewal yet announced, amid claims from some police officials and researchers that the program had worsened the opioid crisis, while other research found consumption sites reduced overdoses.
note: Added missing Feb 8, 2024 national auto-theft summit (salient crime event, previously omitted); fixed overclaim that safer-supply funding 'was not renewed' -- that outcome was only known after the March 31, 2025 expiry, which is after the March 24, 2025 cutoff, so reworded to 'no renewal yet announced'.

summary: Russia's war in Ukraine continued into its fourth year by early 2025. Canada maintained sanctions against Russia, including new sanctions targeting Russian drones and its 'shadow fleet' of tankers. Donald Trump's return to the US presidency in January 2025 brought a more transactional approach to alliances, including public disputes over continued US support for Ukraine and a tense late-February 2025 Oval Office meeting between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Canada's relationship with the US was further strained by Trump's tariffs and repeated statements that Canada should become the 51st American state. At the NATO summit in July 2024, Canada pledged to reach the alliance's target of 2% of GDP on defence spending by 2032, a commitment the new US administration pressed Canada to accelerate.

Canadian inflation continued easing through 2024, allowing the Bank of Canada to begin cutting its policy rate from its 5% peak starting in June 2024, with further cuts continuing into early 2025. To ease cost-of-living pressure, the federal government implemented a temporary GST/HST holiday on groceries and other items from December 14, 2024 to February 15, 2025. Housing affordability and rental costs remained a central concern, with the Federal Housing Advocate's 2024-25 report citing a shortfall of 4.4 million affordable homes across the country.

On April 12, 2024, the federal government released 'Canada's Housing Plan,' an action plan aiming to unlock 3.87 million new homes by 2031, including a minimum of 2 million net new homes, with 53 new and ongoing measures to reduce homebuilding costs and speed up municipal approvals. Through 2024, Ottawa listed additional federal lands for housing development and expanded the Apartment Construction Loan Program. The Federal Housing Advocate's 2024-25 report estimated a shortfall of 4.4 million affordable homes nationally, including 3 million for low-income households.

On October 24, 2024, Immigration Minister Marc Miller announced Canada's 2025-2027 Immigration Levels Plan, reducing permanent resident targets from 500,000 to 395,000 in 2025, 380,000 in 2026 and 365,000 in 2027, citing pressure on housing and social infrastructure. For the first time, the plan set targets to reduce temporary residents (international students and foreign workers) to below 5% of Canada's population by the end of 2026, building on a March 2024 announcement to curb the growth of temporary residents. Starting November 1, 2024, new French- or English-language requirements applied to applicants for post-graduation work permits.

Quebec Premier Francois Legault's government kept its permanent immigration levels at roughly 50,000 for 2024 and 2025, around 60,000-66,500 admissions once other categories were counted, resisting calls from business groups for higher numbers and citing the need to protect the French language. Quebec also announced new French-language testing requirements for temporary foreign workers seeking to stay more than three years. Tensions continued between Quebec and the federal government, which had been pursuing a target of 500,000 annual newcomers before announcing reductions to national immigration levels in October 2024.

theme_name: Year overview (main issues of the moment)
summary: Donald Trump's re-election in November 2024 and subsequent tariffs and repeated calls for Canada to become the 51st US state dominated the period, with 25% US tariffs on Canadian goods taking effect March 4, 2025 and Canada retaliating. Justin Trudeau announced his resignation as Liberal leader on January 6, 2025, after Chrystia Freeland's December 2024 cabinet resignation; Mark Carney won the Liberal leadership on March 9, 2025 and became prime minister on March 14, scrapping the federal consumer carbon tax as his first act. The Liberals had lost byelections in Toronto-St. Paul's and LaSalle-Emard-Verdun in 2024. Ottawa also announced major cuts to immigration targets in October 2024, and the Hogue inquiry released its final report on foreign interference on January 28, 2025. Carney called a snap federal election on March 23, 2025, for April 28.
